prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active peptide form that made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single B041 part for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The scientific case is a continuous discovery chain: Holst on the incretin effect and GLP-1 secretion in humans, Drucker on proglucagon-derived peptide biology and its actions, and Mojsov on the biologically active truncated peptide. That chain led to receptor agonists whose benefit on glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal endpoints has been confirmed in large independent randomized trials. Originality, mechanistic clarity and maturity are all secure, and the discovery fits the Physiology or Medicine remit directly. The agreement of all six round-1 statements is not my reason, since the same members also named attribution as the main weakness. My reason is that this trio credits the discovery side of the chain with the fewest unresolved assumptions.
statement.case_against: The attribution risk remains and round 1 did not remove it. Priority for the active GLP-1 peptide is described as contested, Habener and other early contributors are outside the credited names, and Knudsen's long-acting acylated agonists were decisive for patients and are left out by the three-person limit. None of us can settle the priority record from the permitted material, so the third name rests on a judgement about which step counts as discovery. If the committee decides the prize should honour the therapy as much as the physiology, my configuration is wrong in one name. A single-part prize also leaves the strong CAR-T and UPR cases unrecognised this year, although I do not think they can be added without damaging B041.

responses.point: The chair asks whether the committee will adjudicate the Mojsov and Habener priority record and decide between Mojsov and Knudsen, and whether any citation wording could honour the analogue programme without naming Knudsen.
responses.response: I have changed my view since my opening, where I placed Knudsen in the third slot, and I now hold the trio with Mojsov. The reason is the discovery-versus-development test. Identifying the truncated active peptide is what turned incretin physiology into something a chemist could drug, while the acylated analogues applied that knowledge with new chemistry. I still call Knudsen's step distinct and decisive for patients, and I do not retract that. On priority, I cannot adjudicate Mojsov against Habener from the permitted files. The most I can do is word the citation so it asserts the discovery of the physiology and the active form without a claim of exclusive first identification. I would not write a citation that alludes to the analogues indirectly, because that implies credit we are not giving. If a reliable record showed Mojsov's contribution to be materially secondary to Habener's, I would reopen the third name, and silence on the point should not be read as agreement.

responses.point: Perlmann sees the UPR (B011) as a clean, stable 25-year-old Walter and Mori attribution, and warns that a mistake in the B041 credit would damage an otherwise very strong case.
responses.response: I agree that the Walter and Mori pairing is the cleanest attribution on the list, and that is why B011 stays among my two alternatives. I disagree on how readily it should displace stronger candidates. The mechanism is conceptually deep and replicated for decades, but the link to human disease is still mostly correlative and no therapy rests on it. As a molecular geneticist who works with RNA processing, I see how much weight such a basic-science case needs from evidence of consequence. So I rank it as the second choice only when B041 stands alone and the committee wants a basic cell-biology prize, and I would not trade a B041 name for it. I do share your concern about the B041 credit error. My answer is to keep the citation precise, not to enlarge the part.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius keeps TNF blockade (B044) and CAR-T (B023) as the next strongest cases because each created a clinically confirmed therapeutic modality, and asks whether BCR-ABL and HPV overlap with earlier prizes.
responses.response: I accept the modality argument and apply it to B023 more than to B044. CAR-T made a new class of therapy from genetic engineering of the cell itself, with durable remissions and several approved products. TNF blockade, though clean and mature, is a more familiar case of targeted cytokine neutralisation, and its antibody-engineering and TNF-biology steps lie outside Feldmann and Maini. That is why B044 is not among my two alternatives. For B023 I answer the chair's question directly. I could not support a set with Rosenberg as one of three unless the committee decided that adoptive cell transfer and CAR engineering are one achievement, and I doubt that. Eshhar's absence is a real gap that I would want resolved. On B009 and B010 I agree that the overlap with earlier prizes for oncogene work and for HPV as a cause of cancer argues for setting them aside this year, and I would not use my alternatives on them.

responses.point: El-Manira holds that Knudsen's long-acting acylated agonist programme was decisive for patients, and that the prize could recognise the discovery while the drug history sits in the citation. He calls the long-term safety of chronic therapy still unsettled.
responses.response: I share your view that the drug history belongs in the record, and I agree that Knudsen's programme is decisive for patients. I read it as the application of the discovery, not as a separate discovery, so the prize can acknowledge it only through the phrase that the discoveries made incretin-based treatment possible. On long-term safety I agree with you that data on chronic exposure are still accumulating. I see this as a question about the therapy and not about the discovered mechanism, which large trials have already validated. It should not delay a prize for the physiology, since the prize would not certify the safety of any particular drug. We differ slightly on emphasis, because I would not move toward a four-name or a development-weighted configuration, and the three-person limit settles that for me.

uncertainties: Priority for the active GLP-1 peptide and the position of Habener are still unverified in the permitted material, so the third name rests on a discovery-versus-development judgement and not on an adjudicated record.
Whether Knudsen's analogue programme should be given its own recognition in a later year, since the three-person limit prevents it here.
Whether CAR-T (B023) can be given a defensible laureate set without Eshhar and whether Rosenberg belongs with June and Sadelain.
Whether the UPR (B011) should be preferred over CAR-T as a basic-science alternative, which depends on how much demonstrated patient benefit the committee requires.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have co-authored with Linnarsson and Frisen on topics unrelated to any shortlisted discovery, and I share a Karolinska setting with colleagues. I have no documented collaboration, training relationship or institutional tie to any credited name on the shortlist, and I do not request recusal.
